actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hblemma}{thm:p10-ultrafilter-separation}{proved=annex:p10.stone.1}{Ultrafilter dichotomy and separation}
A proper filter \(U\) is an ultrafilter if and only if, for every
\(a\in B\), exactly one of \(a,\neg a\) belongs to \(U\).
Consequently,
\[
 a\vee b\in U\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\in U\text{ or }b\in U.
\]
Assuming BPIT, if \(F\) is a filter and \(b\notin F\), there is an
ultrafilter \(U\supseteq F\) with \(b\notin U\).
In particular, each nonzero element belongs to an ultrafilter,
and distinct Boolean elements are separated by an ultrafilter.
The trivial Boolean algebra has no ultrafilters.
\end{hblemma}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p10-presheaf-category}{The category of presheaves on a small category}
Fix a category \(\mathcal C\) whose object and arrow sets belong
to the fixed universe.  A presheaf on \(\mathcal C\) is a functor
\[
                         X:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathsf{Set}.
\]
Thus \(u:d\to c\) induces a restriction function
\(X(u):X(c)\to X(d)\).
For \(v:e\to d\), the functor laws are
\[
                    X(1_c)=1_{X(c)},\qquad
                    X(u v)=X(v)X(u).
\]
A map of presheaves \(\alpha:X\to Y\) is a natural
transformation: its functions \(\alpha_c:X(c)\to Y(c)\) satisfy
\[
                         Y(u)\alpha_c=\alpha_d X(u).
\]
Write
\(\widehat{\mathcal C}=[\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathsf{Set}]\)
for their category, with componentwise identities and composition.
The category itself may be large in the fixed universe.

For \(c\in\mathcal C\), the representable presheaf is
\(\mathrm y c=\mathcal C(-,c)\).
An arrow \(u:d\to c\) induces
\[
 \mathrm y(u):\mathrm y d\longrightarrow\mathrm y c,\qquad
 (\mathrm y(u))_e(v)=u v\quad(v:e\to d).
\]
This is the covariant Yoneda assignment on representing objects;
each \(\mathrm y c\) is contravariant in its argument.
\index{presheaf}\index{presheaf category}\index{Yoneda embedding}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p10-presheaf-power-objects}{proved=annex:p10.psh.5}{Classification by a power object}
There are bijections, natural in \(Z\),
\[
 \widehat{\mathcal C}(Z,P(X))
       \cong\widehat{\mathcal C}(Z\times X,\Omega)
       \cong\operatorname{Sub}(Z\times X).
\]
The first is uncurrying, and the second pulls back
\(\mathsf{true}\).  Thus \(k:Z\to P(X)\) classifies exactly
\[
                              (k\times1_X)^*(\in_X).
\]
Conversely, the unique classifying map of a subobject
\(S\hookrightarrow Z\times X\) is \(k=\Lambda(\chi_S)\).
Here a superscript \({}^*\) on subobjects denotes pullback.

At each base object \(c\), classification gives a canonical bijection
\[
                       P(X)(c)\cong
                       \operatorname{Sub}(\mathrm y c\times X).
\]
Under this identification, the restriction along \(u:d\to c\)
sends \(S\subseteq\mathrm y c\times X\) to
\[
 S|u=(\mathrm y u\times1_X)^*S,\qquad
 (S|u)(e)=\{(v,x)\in\mathcal C(e,d)\times X(e):
                                      (u\circ v,x)\in S(e)\}.
\]
The membership components are
\[
 (\in_X)(c)=
   \{(S,x):S\in\operatorname{Sub}(\mathrm y c\times X),\
                         x\in X(c),\ (1_c,x)\in S(c)\},
\]
where the first coordinate uses the same canonical identification.
For \(S\subseteq Z\times X\), its classifying map sends
\(z\in Z(c)\) to the subpresheaf
\[
        S_z(d)=\{(u,x)\in\mathcal C(d,c)\times X(d):
                                      (Z(u)(z),x)\in S(d)\}.
\]
These formulas include \(X=0\) and \(\mathcal C=\varnothing\).
All displayed component and subobject collections are small sets.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p12-cdcl-apparatus}{Conflict-analysis vocabulary}
The name \emph{conflict-driven clause learning} (CDCL) is needed for the search
family that augments DPLL with learned entailed clauses and nonchronological
backtracking; it is not an alias for Method~\ref{def:p12-dpll}.  In the
apparatus below, an \emph{implication graph} has one node for each assigned
literal, annotated by decision level; an edge records use of an antecedent
clause in forcing an implied assignment; and a conflict node records a
falsified clause.  Decision level zero contains assignments made by initial
unit propagation before any branch decision; for \(k\geq 1\), level \(k\)
contains the \(k\)-th active branch decision and every assignment it propagates
before the next decision or a backtrack.  A \emph{unique implication point}
(UIP) is a current-level
node through which every path from the current decision to the conflict passes.
The \emph{first UIP} is the UIP closest to the conflict.  Resolving the
conflict explanation to a first-UIP clause yields an entailed
learned clause.  For a literal in that clause, its level means the decision
level of the currently assigned complementary literal that falsifies it.  A
learned clause is \emph{asserting} when exactly one of its literals is
falsified at the current decision level; that literal is the
\emph{asserting literal}, and the remaining clause literals are
\emph{nonasserting}.  The \emph{backjump level} is the greatest level among
the assigned complements of the nonasserting literals, or zero when there is
no such literal.  Backtracking to that level leaves the asserting literal
unassigned while the others remain false, so the learned clause is unit.
These clause roles are needed to determine this nonchronological return and
are not new object-language literal forms.  Watched literals are a
propagation data structure: two positions in a nonunit clause are monitored so
that the clause need not be revisited until a watched literal becomes false.
A restart discards the current partial assignment while retaining the input
and the selected learned clauses.  For a clause \(C\), reverse unit propagation
holds when unit propagation from the current database together with the
complements of every literal of \(C\) reaches the empty clause.  A clause has
the resolution-asymmetric-tautology property on a pivot \(L\in C\) when, for
every current clause containing \(\neg L\), the corresponding resolvent passes
that reverse-unit-propagation test.  A DRAT log is a sequence of clause
additions satisfying one of those checks and unrestricted deletions, ending
with addition of the empty clause; its independent checker validates the
refutation log, not the solver implementation.  These are metalinguistic
implementation and evidence roles, not new logical rules.  Their exact
distinctions are needed by
Table~\ref{tab:p12-dpll-cdcl} and Figure~\ref{fig:p12-cdcl-conflict}.
\index{conflict-driven clause learning}\index{implication graph}
\index{decision level}\index{unique implication point}\index{first UIP}
\index{asserting clause}\index{asserting literal}\index{backjump level}%
\index{nonasserting literal}\index{watched literal}\index{restart}
\index{reverse unit propagation}
\index{resolution-asymmetric tautology}
\index{DRAT}
\end{hbdefinition}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbmethod}{def:p12-martelli-montanari}{Martelli--Montanari unification}
The exact transformation system is
\hyperref[sheet:unification-first-order]{\texttt{sheet:unification-first-order}}.
Its state invariant is that the current equation multiset has exactly the same
unifiers as the initial multiset, up to the explicit solved substitutions
accumulated by Eliminate. Delete and Decompose preserve syntactic solutions;
Orient changes only equation order; Eliminate composes every remaining
constraint with a forced binding. Clash is unsatisfiable by freeness of the
term algebra, and Occurs fails because no finite term can equal a proper term
containing itself. The method name is necessary to distinguish this finite
syntactic procedure from unification modulo equations or higher-order
unification. It stands as a transformation algorithm, differs through the
occurs check and free-term semantics, and is used in the MGU theorem
\cite{MartelliMontanari1982,BaaderSnyder2001}.
\index{Martelli--Montanari algorithm}\index{occurs check}
\end{hbmethod}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p12-ordered-superposition}{Ordered-superposition saturation}
The calculus is
\hyperref[sheet:ordered-superposition]{\texttt{sheet:ordered-superposition}}.
A clause is redundant in a set \(S\) when it is entailed by strictly smaller
clauses under the fixed ground-clause ordering in the declared redundancy
criterion. A fair saturation derivation eventually performs every persistent
nonredundant eligible inference or makes its conclusion redundant. These names
are needed because unrestricted equality replacement is neither terminating
search nor the cited completeness calculus. They stand as an inference system,
deletion criterion, and scheduling property, differ through the explicit
ordering/selection constraints, and are used in the completeness boundary
\cite{BachmairGanzinger2001,NieuwenhuisRubio2001}.
\index{ordered superposition}\index{saturation}\index{redundancy!superposition}
\end{hbdefinition}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p12-resolution-refinement-roles}{Refinement roles}
A \emph{resolution refinement} is a precisely declared restriction, inference
family, search strategy, or redundancy operation applied around a fixed base
calculus.  The umbrella name is necessary for comparison but does not erase
those four different standings.  For the ordered-resolution surface compared
here, fix a term ordering that is well founded, stable under substitution,
monotone under term contexts, and total on ground terms, together with its
declared extension to literals.  A \emph{literal selection function} maps each
clause to a subset of its negative literals.  A clause literal is
\emph{eligible} when it is selected, or, if that clause has no selected
literal, when it is maximal in the declared literal ordering; ordered
resolution admits only inferences whose resolved literals are eligible after
the unifier is applied.  Thus the ordering restriction and literal selection
are explicit and neither means that the underlying Resolution rule changed.

In Robinson's nucleus/electron
notation for hyperresolution, a nucleus clause \(N\) has designated literals
that are paired with designated complementary literals in electron clauses
\(E_1,\ldots,E_q\); one simultaneous most general unifier makes all pairs
complementary, and the hyperresolvent contains the unpaired literals of all
premises under that unifier.  A concrete positive or negative variant must
also fix the required polarities and factoring convention.

In Slagle's semantic-resolution notation, fix a ground interpretation \(M\).
A \emph{semantic clash} is a finite family
\(\{E_1,\ldots,E_q,N\}\) in which every electron \(E_i\) is false under
\(M\), \(R_1=N\), each \(R_{i+1}\) is an ordinary resolvent of \(R_i\) and
\(E_i\), and the final \(R_{q+1}\) is false under \(M\).  The clause \(N\)
is the nucleus and \(R_{q+1}\) is the \(M\)-resolvent.  This clash condition
is the exact fixed-interpretation eligibility test used here: it restricts
which multi-premise resolution chains are admitted, while every conclusion
remains a syntactic resolution consequence.  It differs from hyperresolution's
polarity restriction and from the support partition below
\cite{Robinson1965,Slagle1967}.

For \emph{set of support}, partition the input clauses into a usable set
\(U\) and a support set \(S\).  The support closure is the least clause set
containing \(S\) and containing the conclusion of every Resolution or
Factoring instance on
\hyperref[sheet:resolution-fol]{\texttt{sheet:resolution-fol}} that has at
least one premise already in that closure and has every other premise in
\(U\) or that closure.  The strategy permits exactly those instances.  With
no deletion or contraction, such a search is \emph{fair} when every permitted
sheet instance is eventually performed after all of its premises have been
generated.  This is a parent-selection strategy, not a new
inference family.

A clause \(C\) \emph{subsumes} \(D\) exactly
when some term substitution \(\rho\) satisfies \(C\rho\subseteq D\), licensing
deletion of \(D\) as redundant.  None is synonymous with unrestricted
resolution, and each later completeness claim needs its own hypotheses.
\index{ordered resolution}\index{hyperresolution}\index{hyperresolvent}
\index{semantic resolution}
\index{literal selection function}\index{eligible literal}
\index{semantic clash}\index{nucleus}\index{electron}
\index{M-resolvent}
\index{set of support}\index{support closure}\index{fair search}
\index{subsumption}
\end{hbdefinition}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p12-nelson-oppen}{cited=NelsonOppen1979}{Nelson--Oppen combination boundary}
Let quantifier-free inputs be purified into component signatures that are
disjoint apart from equality and explicitly shared sorts.  Suppose each
component theory has a decision procedure for its quantifier-free fragment and
is stably infinite on the shared sorts.  Then satisfiability in their union is
decidable by exchanging compatible equality arrangements on the shared
variables.  For convex components, communication of individually implied
equalities suffices; nonconvex components require disjunctive case splitting.
Disjointness supplies sound separation, but without the stated
stable-infiniteness hypothesis this completeness conclusion does not follow.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p12-pts-lambda-cube}{Pure type system and lambda cube}
A \emph{pure type system} has Barendregt's specification
\(S=(\mathcal S,\mathcal A,\mathcal R)\), where \(\mathcal S\) is a set of
sorts, \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal S\mathbin{\times}\mathcal S\) is a set
of sort-typing axioms \(s_1{:}s_2\), and
\(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal S\mathbin{\times}\mathcal S
\mathbin{\times}\mathcal S\) is a set of triples declaring which
dependent-product sorts may be formed: \((s_1,s_2,s_3)\in\mathcal R\)
licenses a dependent product of sort \(s_3\) when its domain has sort \(s_1\)
and its codomain, under the bound variable, has sort \(s_2\).  Its calculus is
denoted
\(\lambda S=\lambda(\mathcal S,\mathcal A,\mathcal R)\).  The identifier
\(\mathsf{PTS}\) names this parameterized family, not one theorem prover.

For the \emph{lambda cube}, fix
\(\mathcal S=\{\ast,\Box\}\),
\(\mathcal A=\{\ast{:}\Box\}\), and the base product pair
\((\ast,\ast)\), where Barendregt abbreviates
\((s_1,s_2,s_2)\) by \((s_1,s_2)\).  The eight vertices arise by adjoining
any subset of \((\ast,\Box)\), \((\Box,\ast)\), and
\((\Box,\Box)\).  These axes respectively permit types to depend on terms,
terms to depend on types, and types to depend on types.  Their standing as
independent formation choices distinguishes the cube from a linear strength
ordering and is used in Table~\ref{tab:p12-lambda-cube}.  Barendregt's
strongest-corner identifier is \(\lambda\mathrm P\omega=\lambda\mathrm C\),
the Calculus of Constructions; it is not CIC
\cite{Barendregt1992,CoquandHuet1988}.
\index{pure type system}\index{lambda cube}\index{Calculus of Constructions}
\end{hbdefinition}

dependent products, dependent sums, identity types, and a cumulative universe
discipline, extended in the cited presentation by the univalence axiom and

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-hilbert-deduction}{proved=annex:p2.calc.2}{Deduction theorem for the Hilbert calculus}
For every set \(\Gamma\) and all formulas \(\varphi,\psi\) of the
\(\{\neg,\to\}\)-fragment,
\[
 \Gamma\cup\{\varphi\}\derives_{\mathsf H_{\mathsf{CPL}}}\psi
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Gamma\derives_{\mathsf H_{\mathsf{CPL}}}(\varphi\to\psi).
\]
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-calculi-derivability-equivalence}{cited=Kleene1952}{Derivability equivalence of the classical calculi}
Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite set of full-language propositional formulas and
let \(\varphi\) be a full-language formula.  View \(\Gamma\) as a multiset
with multiplicity one when it forms a sequent antecedent.  Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Gamma\entails\varphi
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Gamma\derives_{\mathsf{ND}_{\mathsf{CPL}}}\varphi\\
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{the sequent }\Gamma\Rightarrow\varphi
   \text{ is derivable in }\mathsf{LK}_{\mathsf{CPL}}\\
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{tr}_{\mathsf H}[\Gamma]
   \derives_{\mathsf H_{\mathsf{CPL}}}
   \operatorname{tr}_{\mathsf H}(\varphi).
\end{aligned}
\]
The natural-deduction and sequent presentations are due to Gentzen; see
\cite{Gentzen1934a}.  A standard classical metatheoretic treatment is
\cite{Kleene1952}.
\end{hbtheorem}

presentations.version: Current identified handbook source presentation; file hashes fix its version

original_goal_and_notes.item: Duality theorem for propositional logic
original_goal_and_notes.notes: cross-cutting list

required_components: Define the selected Boolean formula dualization, including constants when admitted.
Prove its exact semantic identity and the resulting identity/validity/contradiction correspondence.
Keep the transformation distinct from merely negating a formula.

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-propositional-duality}{proved=annex:p2.1.8}{Duality theorem}
Let \(\bar v(p)=1-v(p)\).  For every NNF presentation \(\alpha\),
\[
 v\entails\alpha^{\mathrm d}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \bar v\not\entails\alpha.
\]
Consequently dualization is an involution, preserves logical equivalence,
exchanges valid formulas with unsatisfiable formulas, and exchanges CNF with
DNF.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p2.1.8}{thm:p02-propositional-duality}{Duality theorem}
\begin{proof}
Induct on the displayed NNF presentation \(\alpha\).  If \(\alpha\) is a
positive literal \(p\), then
\(v\entails p\) iff \(\bar v\not\entails p\).  If it is \(\neg p\), then
\(v\entails\neg p\) iff \(v(p)=0\), iff
\(\bar v(p)=1\), iff \(\bar v\not\entails\neg p\).  The two unit
cases follow from \(\bottom^{\mathrm d}=\topv\) and
\(\topv^{\mathrm d}=\bottom\).  For conjunction,
\[
 v\entails(\beta\land\gamma)^{\mathrm d}
 \quad\text{iff}\quad
 v\entails\beta^{\mathrm d}\text{ or }v\entails\gamma^{\mathrm d}
 \quad\text{iff}\quad
 \bar v\not\entails\beta\land\gamma,
\]
by the induction hypotheses; the disjunction case is dual.  This proves the
displayed semantic identity.

The recursive clauses also give \((\alpha^{\mathrm d})^{\mathrm d}=\alpha\)
by structural induction.  If \(\alpha\Leftrightarrow\beta\), apply the
semantic identity to \(\bar v\) for each \(v\) to obtain
\(\alpha^{\mathrm d}\Leftrightarrow\beta^{\mathrm d}\); the converse follows
from involution.  If \(\alpha\) is valid, the identity makes
\(\alpha^{\mathrm d}\) false under every \(v\).  Conversely, if the dual is
unsatisfiable, apply the identity with \(v=\bar u\) to show that every \(u\)
satisfies \(\alpha\).  Finally, the syntactic clauses swap every outer
conjunction with disjunction, every clause-disjunction with a conjunction of
the same literals, and the two empty units; hence they exchange CNF and DNF.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}
